question.prompt:
The radius of the smallest circle containing the symmetric figure composed of \(3\) unit squares shown is:

[Figure 1](figures/1972_AMC_12_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The symmetry suggests pairing the left and right corners. These pairs give a lower bound that applies even when the circle's center is off the symmetry axis.

[Figure 1](figures/1972_AMC_12_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

Place the bottom corners at \((-1,0)\) and \((1,0)\). The upper square then has top corners \((-\tfrac12,2)\) and \((\tfrac12,2)\). Let a containing circle have center \((s,t)\) and radius \(R\).

Each corner's squared distance from the center is at most \(R^2\), so the average for either pair is also at most \(R^2\). The distance formula gives
\[
R^2\ge s^2+1+t^2\ge1+t^2,
\]
and
\[
R^2\ge s^2+\frac14+(2-t)^2
\ge\frac14+(2-t)^2.
\]
Moving the center upward increases its distance to the bottom pair and decreases its distance to the top pair while it stays between their levels. This suggests balancing the two bounds:
\[
1+t^2=\frac14+(2-t)^2,
\qquad 4t=\frac{13}{4},
\qquad t=\frac{13}{16}.
\]
This balance really gives a universal minimum. If \(t\ge13/16\), then \(1+t^2\ge425/256\). If \(t\le13/16\), then \(2-t\ge19/16\), so \(\tfrac14+(2-t)^2\ge425/256\). Thus every containing circle satisfies \(R^2\ge425/256\).

To show that this bound is attainable, take the center \((0,13/16)\). Every point in the bottom two squares satisfies \(|x|\le1\) and \(0\le y\le1\), so its squared distance is at most
\[
1+\left(\frac{13}{16}\right)^2=\frac{425}{256}.
\]
Every point in the upper square satisfies \(|x|\le\tfrac12\) and \(1\le y\le2\), giving squared distance at most
\[
\frac14+\left(\frac{19}{16}\right)^2=\frac{425}{256}.
\]
Consequently this circle contains the entire figure, and the smallest radius is
\[
\boxed{R=\frac{\sqrt{425}}{16}=\frac{5\sqrt{17}}{16}},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
solutions.title: Compare distances to paired corners
